summaries.example: Imagine making a short movie with a tablet. You draw some pictures, ask a computer program to change their colors, and show the movie on a screen. The computer is not just a tool sitting nearby: its storing, changing, or displaying information helps make the artwork what it is. A video game can work similarly, but the player may also help create what appears on the screen.
summaries.summary: The philosophy of digital art asks what makes computer-dependent art special and how we should understand it. Digital art is not one single kind of art. It can include pictures, movies, music, stories, games, online projects, and art linked to places. Computers store information in countable digital patterns, often using 0s and 1s. This can make copying, changing, and combining media easier. But the fact that a computer can store pictures, sounds, and words in a common code does not mean that all art is the same. A film is still a film, and a story is still a story. Digital tools also create new artistic choices and problems. Artists may need to decide how much control users have, whether a work should have one display or many, and how computer automation affects creativity. Some works use people’s movements or locations to change what happens. The main lesson is that technology matters, but it does not replace artistic choices or the need to interpret artworks carefully.
key_ideas: Digital art includes many forms, such as digital photographs, electronic music, films, online art, chatbot writing, and video games.
A work may be made digitally but shown in a non-digital way, or it may be both made and shown digitally.
Digital systems use separate, countable settings, while analog systems can change smoothly. Digital pictures can still look smooth to people.
Computers make some artistic actions easier, but artists still make choices about what to keep, change, and present.
Some digital artworks respond to users. Their displays may change according to the user’s actions.
Art connected to locations can join real places with virtual information and invite people to explore or participate.
summaries.why_it_matters: Digital tools are part of everyday life, so they shape how people make, share, and experience art. Thinking about digital art helps us notice that a screen is not the whole artwork. The program, instructions, user actions, display, and setting may all matter. It also helps us ask fair questions about copying, creativity, authorship, and access to technology.

important_terms.definition: Art that depends importantly on computer processing when it is made, shown, or both.
A way of storing information with separate, countable values, often using 0s and 1s.
A way of representing things with smoothly changing values, such as the changing height of liquid in a thermometer.
A set of instructions that tells a computer how to carry out a task.
When a user’s actions help produce what an artwork shows or does.

questions_to_think_about: Does an artwork have to be shown on a screen to count as digital art?
How might a video game be different from a movie because of what the player does?
If a computer makes many possible pictures, who should get credit for the artwork?
Can a digital copy be just as important as the first version?

summaries.example: Consider a branching digital film in which viewers choose whether a character enters a building or walks away. The artist supplies the images, code, rules, and possible paths, but the viewer’s prescribed choice helps determine the particular display. This differs from a standard digital photograph: its pixels may look slightly different on different screens, yet those changes do not alter the photograph’s structure. The film’s variability is part of how the work is designed.
summaries.summary: The philosophy of digital art examines artworks that crucially depend on computer processing and asks how digital technology affects artistic identity, appreciation, production, and presentation. The category includes digital cinema, photography, painting, music, literature, games, net art, AI-generated works, and location-based projects. A work can be produced digitally yet presented through traditional instruments, stage performance, or film, while other works are digital in both production and display. The analog-digital distinction helps explain why digital systems are discrete and replicable, whereas analog systems are dense or continuously variable. Yet the visible appearance of a digital image may be smooth, since technological distinctions can be finer than human perception. This complicates simple claims that digital images are aesthetically poorer than analog ones. Digital technology also does not make artistic media irrelevant. A film converted into another format remains a film rather than becoming the other artwork, and the artistic use of binary code can constitute a digital medium with sub-media. The ontology of digital art depends partly on artist-sanctioned presentation rules, algorithms, hardware, software, and user participation. Interactive works are distinctive because users help generate prescribed displays; some have repeatable variations, while others develop irreversibly. These cases connect digital art with debates about creativity, agency, and whether generative AI can participate in artistic collaboration. Locative art extends these issues into physical and virtual spaces, often combining play, social participation, and practical goals.
key_ideas: “Digital art” is a broad category. Computer processing can occur during making, presentation, or both, and a work made digitally need not be displayed digitally.

The analog-digital distinction concerns the structure of representational systems. Digital systems use finite differentiation, while analog systems involve continuous variation. Digital images can appear continuous because sampling differences may fall below human perception.

Digital replication does not by itself determine an artwork’s identity or whether it has multiple instances. Artists’ presentation instructions can make a work singular, repeatable, or otherwise structured.
The common binary code of computers does not eliminate artistic media. Digital art can contain nested media, such as digital visual art, and artworks remain shaped by how their materials are used.

Interactivity involves prescribed user contributions, not merely accidental differences in brightness, hardware, or performance. Some interactive works permit repeatable displays; others develop through states that cannot be revisited.

Digital art raises questions about creativity and attribution. Human artists may design and guide generative systems, while some theorists ask whether advanced AI systems can count as creative partners rather than only tools.
summaries.why_it_matters: Digital art challenges familiar assumptions about originals, copies, media, authorship, and audience roles. Understanding its philosophy helps us avoid two oversimplifications: that computers merely make old art faster, or that digital technology makes all artistic categories disappear. It also gives us tools for assessing interactive and AI-assisted works without assuming in advance who—or what—deserves creative credit.

important_terms.definition: Art whose production or presentation depends in a significant way on computer-based encoding, storage, or processing.

A representational system with sufficiently distinct syntactic and semantic types that users can determine which type an item belongs to; digital systems are associated with discrete, replicable information.
A representational system whose possible types vary continuously and are not separated into clearly distinct classes; pictures and thermometer readings are important examples.
The philosophical study of what an artwork is made of, how it is individuated, and what makes one work the same work across displays or instances.
A procedure or rule-governed set of operations that a computer can execute, including conditional steps and branching.
A work is interactive when it prescribes that users’ actions help generate its display; not every digital work is interactive, and not every interactive work is digital.
A possible combination of structural and aesthetic properties that an artwork can present. Highly variable interactive works may have more than one such type.
Appreciation that considers how an artwork’s medium enables, limits, or shapes its effects and artistic choices.

questions_to_think_about: If a digital image can be copied perfectly, what could make one artwork singular rather than multiply instantiable?
Is a user’s unplanned action enough for interactivity, or must the artwork prescribe the action’s role?
Does the ability to translate images into sounds or text show that digital art has no medium? Why might that inference fail?
When an AI system produces something novel and valuable, what further condition might be needed before calling it creative?
Should an interactive artwork be understood mainly as an object, a process, or a combination of both?

summaries.example: Suppose you design an online mystery game. You write the story, choose the clues, and program several endings. Players decide which clues to follow, so their actions help create the version they see. That is stronger than simply viewing the same picture on different phones, because differences in screen brightness do not change the picture’s basic structure. The game’s rules make the players’ choices part of the artwork.
summaries.summary: Digital art is art that depends importantly on computer processing in its creation or presentation. The category includes familiar forms such as digital photography and film, but also electronic music, online literature, video games, chatbot fiction, AI-generated images, and locative art. The source distinguishes production from presentation: a work may be created with software and then performed or shown in a traditional format, while a purely digital work is made and displayed through digital systems. Philosophers also examine the analog-digital distinction. Digital systems use separate, recognizable values, whereas analog systems allow continuous variation. This explains why computers can copy and process information reliably, although digital images may still look smooth because their tiny differences are not noticeable to human viewers. The ease of copying does not settle what an artwork is. An artist’s instructions can specify whether a work is one physical installation, a repeatable online work, or an interactive system. Interactivity is especially important in digital art, but it is not automatic: a user must have a prescribed role in generating the display. Games may offer many possible paths or endings, while small changes between screens do not make an ordinary image interactive. Digital art also raises questions about medium and creativity. A common computer code can store images, sound, and text, but the way that code is artistically used still matters. Generative AI makes the question of creative agency even harder by separating the person who designs and guides a system from the system’s own outputs. Locative art adds physical location, virtual information, community participation, and sometimes practical or social aims to the discussion.
key_ideas: Digital art is a large family, not one style. It can include movies, photos, music, stories, games, online art, AI art, and art connected to physical locations.
A digital work can be made digitally but presented without a screen. What matters is how computer processing is important to the work.

Digital systems separate information into distinct values. Analog systems represent changing values more continuously. This difference is about how information is organized, not simply whether something looks pixelated.
Copying is easy for digital information, but an artwork’s identity still depends on artistic instructions, presentation rules, and the kind of work it is.
Interactive art gives users a planned role in producing the display. A video game may have many possible outcomes, while a normal digital photograph has one basic display type.
Digital tools change what artists can do, but they do not remove the importance of artistic decisions or the medium in which an artwork works.
summaries.why_it_matters: Much of today’s culture is made with computers, so these questions affect how we judge films, games, online projects, AI works, and digital images. Philosophy helps us look beyond the novelty of technology. It asks what the artist controls, what the audience contributes, how copies relate to originals, and how a work’s medium shapes what counts as a successful artistic choice.

important_terms.definition: Art that relies importantly on computers to create, store, change, or present information such as images, sounds, numbers, or text.
A system that uses separate values or categories, rather than a smooth range of possible values.
A system in which values can vary continuously, with no simple set of separate steps between them.
The question of what an artwork is, what belongs to it, and how it remains the same across different presentations.
A rule-based procedure that tells a computer how to process information or respond to conditions.
A feature of an artwork in which users’ prescribed actions help produce what the artwork displays.
The particular version of an artwork’s visible, audible, or structural features that can occur during a presentation.

questions_to_think_about: If a poem is written in a word processor but performed on stage, in what sense is it digital?
Why might a movie remain a movie even if its images are translated into another form?
What is the difference between a user changing an artwork and merely changing the way it looks on a device?
Can a computer program be part of a creative partnership with a human artist?
How might an artwork connected to a neighborhood affect how people understand that place?
